title: Paper Rockets: Why Fins Keep Them Flying Straight
summary:
Can you build a rocket out of paper and launch it with a straw and a deep breath? This experiment shows you how — and teaches you why some rockets fly straight while others spin out of control.

You start by making tube-shaped rockets from paper and tape, then launching them by blowing into a drinking straw. The challenge is simple: can you make the rocket that flies the farthest? First, try a rocket with no fins. It may fly straight at first, but it quickly spirals out of control, tumbling through the air and fluttering to the ground almost like a leaf falling from a tree.

Now add fins and launch again. The finned rocket should fly straight and travel much farther. That is because the fins keep the rocket stable, holding it pointed in the same direction. If the rocket starts to turn a little, the fins help turn it back. Without fins, a small turn grows quickly until the rocket loses control completely.

The same idea applies to everything that flies, from airplanes to birds. Just as training wheels keep a bicycle steady, fins keep a flying object steady. Real rockets and missiles usually have triangular fins at their bases, and arrows work the same way. The fins make sure the rocket's center of pressure — the point where air resistance acts — sits behind its center of mass, the point where all its mass is concentrated.

Each launch is a small experiment. Comparing a finless rocket with a finned one shows how a tiny change in shape can change how far — and how straight — a rocket flies.
why_it_matters: Trying small changes and watching what happens is how scientists learn, and this experiment shows how a tiny change in shape can change how something flies.

keywords.explanation: Stable means steady and not wobbling or falling over.
Spirals means turning round and round while moving, like a corkscrew.
Triangular means shaped like a triangle, with three sides.
The center of pressure is the point where air resistance acts on a flying object.
The center of mass is the point where all of an object's mass is concentrated.
Air resistance is the push of the air against something moving through it.

background_read: A rocket flies through the air, and the shape of the rocket decides whether it stays pointed in one direction or tumbles.
Fins are flat parts at the back of a rocket that steady it, a bit like training wheels steady a bicycle.
When a rocket starts to turn, its fins push against the air and help turn it back, so a small wobble does not grow into a spin.
The same idea works for everything that flies, from real rockets and arrows to airplanes and birds, because fins keep the point where air pushes behind the point where the weight is centered.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A paper rocket launched with a straw flies straight when it has fins and spins out of control when it does not.
KEY EVENT: An experiment compares a finless paper rocket with a finned one to see which flies farthest.
├─ HOW: Tube-shaped rockets are made from paper and tape and launched by blowing into a drinking straw.
├─ NO FINS: The rocket may fly straight at first, then spirals out of control and flutters to the ground like a falling leaf.
└─ WITH FINS: The rocket flies straight and much farther because the fins keep it stable.
WHY IT WORKS: The fins keep the rocket's center of pressure, where air resistance acts, behind its center of mass.
